argument: Hume argues that denying an objective, cosmic standard of beauty doesn't mean every person's judgment of art is equally valid; those are two separate questions people often conflate. Just as we consult a trained expert for a scientific disagreement even without an absolute cosmic standard, Hume thinks a cultivated 'ideal critic' can judge art better than an untrained person. In his essay 'Of the Standard of Taste,' he lays out five qualities such a critic needs, while also warning against common false criteria people mistake for genuine markers of quality, like nostalgia, novelty, and complexity.
keyIdeas: People often confuse two separate questions: whether there's an objective cosmic standard of beauty, and whether people's ability to judge art well is equally developed; a 'no' to the first doesn't mean 'no' to the second.

Hume justifies the idea of an ideal critic by analogy to scientific expertise: years of cultivated skill can make one person's judgment more reliable than another's, even without an absolute standard to measure against.

Common but faulty criteria people use to justify their taste include nostalgia (which reveals personal history, not quality in the art), false novelty (mistaking unfamiliarity for genuine originality), and complexity (which doesn't necessarily imply superiority over simplicity).

Hume's five qualities of the ideal critic are: delicate sentiment (perceiving fine details accurately), practice, comparison (context from wide exposure to other art), freedom from prejudice (about the artist, not just the art), and strong sense (basic sensory access to the work).

Hume notes a near-paradox: though taste seems deeply subjective, truly great art (Shakespeare, da Vinci, Homer) has a timeless consistency that even more 'objective' fields like science and philosophy lack, since their giants get superseded.

terms.def: Hume's essay arguing that while there's no objective standard of beauty, some critical judgments are still better than others.
Hume's concept of a tastemaker whose cultivated skills (comparable to a scientist's expertise) make their aesthetic judgments more reliable than an untrained person's.
The ability to perceive the finer details and choices in a work of art accurately, without missing details or reading meaning into things that aren't there.
The view, which Hume rejects as incomplete, that no art is better or worse than any other on a cosmic level, purely personal preference.
Basic, undistorted sensory access to a work of art, the foundational requirement before any other critical skill can apply.
